title: Paragraphs and topic sentences
examples: How do I know if my paragraph has only one main idea?
What are some good linking words to use between my sentences?
Should I put the topic sentence at the beginning of my paragraph?

explain.say: A paragraph should talk about only one main idea.
The topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about.

draw.text: Topic sentence states the main idea.

explain.say: Supporting details give examples that prove your topic sentence is true.
Linking words help your sentences flow smoothly together.
For example, a paragraph about dogs might discuss their playful nature.
In real life, when you write about your favorite season, keep it focused.

faq.a: It is the sentence that tells the reader the main point of your paragraph. You can think of it as a mini-summary for the whole paragraph.
asks: Where do I put the main idea?
What should the first sentence do?

faq.q: How many ideas can fit in one paragraph?
faq.a: A good paragraph should stick to only one main idea. If you have two ideas, you need two separate paragraphs.
asks: Can I mix ideas in one paragraph?
Do I need a new paragraph for every new idea?

faq.a: Linking words are words like 'also' or 'however' that connect your sentences. They help your writing sound natural and easy to read.
asks: How do I make my writing flow better?

faq.q: Does the topic sentence have to be the first sentence?
faq.a: While it is often best to put it first, you can sometimes put it later. Just make sure the reader knows the main point.
asks: Is the topic sentence always first?
Can I move the main idea sentence?

faq.q: What if my details don't support my topic sentence?
faq.a: If your details do not support your main idea, you need to change either the details or the topic sentence. They must match!
asks: How do I make my evidence fit my point?

facts: A topic sentence controls the focus of the entire paragraph.
Supporting details give evidence for the topic sentence.
Linking words create smooth transitions between sentences.
Each paragraph should focus on one single main idea.

quiz.say: Which sentence best controls the main idea of a paragraph about rainforests?
quiz.show: A. Rainforests have many types of animals.

options.show: C. The air is very hot and humid.
options.say: C. The air is very hot and humid.

options.show: D. They are very green and wet.
options.say: D. They are very green and wet.

options.show: A. Rainforests have many types of animals.
options.say: A. Rainforests have many types of animals.

options.show: B. Monkeys swing through the canopy.
options.say: B. Monkeys swing through the canopy.

quiz.why: This sentence clearly states the main subject, which is the variety of animals in rainforests.

wrong.0: This describes the climate, which is a different idea from the animal variety.
wrong.1: This is a general description, not a clear topic sentence.
wrong.3: This is only one detail, not the main idea for the whole paragraph.

quiz.say: If a paragraph discusses only the benefits of recycling, what is its main idea?

options.show: Talking about plastic and glass separately.
options.say: Talking about plastic and glass separately.

options.show: Starting with an example and ending with a conclusion.
options.say: Starting with an example and ending with a conclusion.

quiz.why: The paragraph must stick to just one topic, like recycling's benefits, not mixing it with another topic.

wrong.1: Mixing topics makes the paragraph unclear and confusing for the reader.
wrong.2: These are examples, but the paragraph needs one overarching point to connect them.
wrong.3: While good, the structure must still support one central, controlling idea.

quiz.say: Which linking word best connects two ideas about the importance of exercise?
quiz.why: The word 'also' adds another supporting point that agrees with the previous one.

wrong.0: This word shows a cause, which is not the relationship needed here.
wrong.2: This word shows a result, which is different from just adding more information.
wrong.3: This word shows a contrast, suggesting the next idea disagrees with the last one.
